extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and practitioners handling discovery (depositions and interrogatories) in TTAB inter partes proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive rules for taking, objecting to, certifying, serving, and using depositions (oral and on written questions) and for serving and responding to interrogatories in Trademark Trial and Appeal Board inter partes proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of time for depositions on written questions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may extend any of the time periods specified in 37 CFR § 2.124(d)(1) (time periods for serving cross questions, redirect questions, recross questions, objections, and substitute questions) on motion for good cause or on its own initiative to allow for orderly completion of depositions on written questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 37 CFR § 2.124(d)(2) regarding suspension of proceedings for testimonial depositions on written questions. Extensions permit orderly completion when multiple rounds of questions/objections are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mailing and service of notice and questions (written questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within 10 days after the last date when questions, objections, or substitute questions may be served, the deposing party must mail a copy of the notice and copies of all the questions to the officer designated in the notice and serve a copy on every adverse party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict 10-day timing; failure to mail/serve properly could affect validity of deposition. See 37 CFR § 2.124(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer must record each answer immediately after corresponding question
rubrics_metrics.description: The officer designated in the notice shall take the testimony and shall record each answer immediately after the corresponding question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the required form of depositions on written questions; see 37 CFR § 2.124(e) and TBMP § 703.01(i) for related form requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service of written objections to questions and right to serve substitute questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Written objections to questions propounded for a deposition on written questions may be served on the propounding party; any party who objects must serve a copy on every other adverse party. Substitute questions may be served on the objecting party within ten days of service of the objections and shall be served on every other adverse party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow 37 CFR § 2.124(d)(1) for timing; substitute questions preserve the objecting party's ability to refine the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections to questions/answers may be considered at final hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to questions and answers in depositions on written questions generally are considered by the Board (unless waived) at final hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If objections have been overcome by revised questions, file and serve notice identifying objections no longer to be considered. Objections not maintained in the final hearing brief may be deemed waived (see TBMP §§ 707.03(c), 707.04).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification and mailing of deposition transcript by officer
rubrics_metrics.description: After taking a deposition on written questions, the officer must certify the transcript and mail the certified transcript and exhibits to the party who took the deposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 37 CFR § 2.124(e) and 37 CFR § 2.123(f); certification is required before the transcript is sent to the propounding party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service, correction, and making deposition of record
rubrics_metrics.description: The party who took the deposition must promptly serve a copy of the transcript, documentary exhibits, and duplicates or photographs of physical exhibits on every adverse party, and must assure that the transcript is correct (see § 2.125(b)). If a discovery deposition is to be made of record, follow 37 CFR § 2.120(j).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt service and ensuring transcript accuracy are the deposing party's responsibilities. See TBMP § 703.01(m)-(n) and TBMP § 704.09 for making depositions of record and error correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility of depositions on written questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Depositions on written questions are cumbersome and deprive face-to-face confrontation, but may be the only means to take a deposition in a foreign country, may be less expensive, and often more convenient for the witness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider tradeoffs (cumbersomeness vs. necessity/convenience) when choosing between written and oral depositions. See TBMP § 703.02(m).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible bases for discovery deposition objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to discovery depositions include errors/irregularities in the notice, manner of taking the deposition, form of a question or answer, the oath or affirmation, a party's conduct, disqualification of an officer, and objections as to competency, relevancy, or materiality of testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(c)(2) and 32(d); identify the specific category of objection and act promptly to avoid waiver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of objections to notice of deposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to errors and irregularities in a notice of the taking of a discovery deposition must be promptly served in writing on the party giving the notice; objections not promptly served are waived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If objectionable, raise notice defects immediately; compare prior TTAB decisions re facial sufficiency vs curable defects and seek telephone conference with Board attorney if needed (see Sunrider Corp. v. Raats).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections to disqualification of officer must be timely
rubrics_metrics.description: An objection to the taking of a discovery deposition because of disqualification of the officer is waived unless made before the deposition begins, or as soon thereafter as the disqualification becomes known or could have been discovered with reasonable diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fed. R. Civ. P. 32(d)(2). Raise officer-disqualification issues promptly or risk waiver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and limits of objections during deposition
rubrics_metrics.description: An objection must be stated concisely and in a nonargumentative and nonsuggestive manner. A person may instruct a deponent not to answer only when necessary to preserve a privilege, enforce a limitation ordered by the court, or to present a motion under Rule 30(d)(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid argumentative or suggestive objections during the deposition; use instructions to preserve privilege or seek court/Board relief when necessary (Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(c)(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Competency/relevance objections not automatically waived
rubrics_metrics.description: An objection to a deponent’s competence—or to the competence, relevance, or materiality of testimony—is not waived by a failure to make the objection before or during the deposition, unless the ground could have been corrected at that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fed. R. Civ. P. 32(d)(3)(A). If the objectionable ground could have been cured, timely objection is required to avoid waiver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections to errors/irregularities at deposition can be waived if untimely
rubrics_metrics.description: An objection to an error or irregularity at an oral examination is waived if it relates to the manner of taking the deposition, the form of a question or answer, the oath or affirmation, a party’s conduct, or other matters that might have been corrected at that time, and it is not timely made during the deposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fed. R. Civ. P. 32(d)(3)(B). Seasonably raise curable procedural objections during the deposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to handle an improper question during deposition
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party believes a question is improper, it may state its objection concisely and nonargumentatively; ordinarily, questions objected to should be answered subject to the objection, except where privilege or protective order applies and the witness may properly refuse to answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answering subject to objection preserves the record; privilege, protective-order grounds, or court-ordered limits may justify refusal to answer. Preserve objections for final hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of objections for final hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to discovery deposition questions should be preserved and argued in the briefs at final hearing; objections not maintained in a brief at final hearing may be considered waived by the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely making objections at deposition is insufficient—renew and identify objections specifically in final-hearing briefs (see cases such as Fischer Gesellschaft m.b.H. v. Molnar and Wet Seal Inc. v. FD Management Inc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Options when witness refuses to answer
rubrics_metrics.description: If a witness refuses to answer during a discovery deposition, the propounding party may complete the deposition and file a motion with the Board to compel; if the deposition is taken pursuant to a subpoena, the party may also apply to the federal district court in the deposition jurisdiction for an order compelling answers (35 U.S.C. § 24).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motion to compel is available for discovery depositions but not testimonial depositions before the Board; seek district-court subpoena enforcement when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of refusal to answer in testimony depositions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a testimony deposition witness refuses to answer and the Board later finds the objection not well taken, the Board may presume the answer would have been unfavorable to the refusing party or may reduce the probative value of the witness's testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because no motion to compel is available for testimony depositions, refusals can be adverse to the refusing party at final hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery deposition vs testimony deposition: scope and timing differences
rubrics_metrics.description: A discovery deposition is a broad discovery device (may seek information that would be inadmissible at trial if reasonably calculated to lead to admissible evidence) taken during the discovery period; a testimony deposition is a narrower device used to present evidence during a party's assigned testimony period and is limited to evidence admissible under applicable rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery depositions may be taken on notice alone; testimony depositions of an adverse party (unless voluntary) require a district-court subpoena. Consider admissibility and timing when choosing deposition type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of discovery depositions in the evidentiary record
rubrics_metrics.description: A discovery deposition does not form part of the evidentiary record unless a party entitled to offer it into evidence files the deposition together with a notice of reliance during the party’s testimony period; offering a discovery deposition into evidence is voluntary, not mandatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See TBMP § 704.09 for introducing discovery depositions into evidence; discovery depositions of nonparty witnesses may require compelling circumstances or consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimony depositions become part of the record when filed
rubrics_metrics.description: Every testimony deposition taken must be filed, and when filed, becomes part of the record; a notice of reliance is not necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See TBMP § 703.01(l). Ensure testimony depositions are timely filed to be in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: When interrogatories may be served
rubrics_metrics.description: For inter partes proceedings commenced on or after November 1, 2007, written interrogatories may be served on any other party during the discovery period only if the serving party previously served or concurrently serves its initial disclosures, absent a stipulation, granted motion, or Board order to the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 37 CFR § 2.120(a)(3) and TBMP § 403.01. Interrogatories may not be served on non-parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of interrogatories
rubrics_metrics.description: Interrogatories may seek any information discoverable under Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b). An otherwise proper interrogatory is not necessarily objectionable merely because it requires an opinion or contention relating to fact or law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Fed. R. Civ. P. 33(a)(2). Questions asking for legal conclusions (e.g., whether marks are confusingly similar) may be required to be answered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical limit on interrogatories
rubrics_metrics.description: The total number of written interrogatories a party may serve on another in a proceeding shall not exceed 75, counting subparts, except the Board may allow additional interrogatories on motion showing good cause or by stipulation of the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A motion for leave to serve additional interrogatories must be filed and granted prior to service and accompanied by copies of interrogatories already served and proposed additional ones. See 37 CFR § 2.120(d)(1) and TBMP § 519.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogatory limit applies to entire proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: The 75-interrogatory limit applies to the total interrogatories served by one party on another over the entire proceeding, not per set of interrogatories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve interrogatory count for follow-ups; multiple sets count cumulatively toward the 75-limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: No automatic extra interrogatories for multiple marks/counterclaims
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule does not provide extra interrogatories where more than one mark is pleaded or where there is a counterclaim; propounding party may request answers with respect to each involved mark, and the interrogatories are counted the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceedings with multiple marks or counterclaims may, however, be unusually complex and that fact will be considered on motions for additional interrogatories (good cause).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting subparts and compound questions as separate interrogatories
rubrics_metrics.description: Each subpart within an interrogatory is counted as a separate interrogatory regardless of separate designation. If a set contains 75 separately designated questions but actually contains more than 75 questions, the Board will count by substance. Compound or combined questions not designated as subparts will be counted by substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an interrogatory contains initial question plus conditional follow-ups, count each as separate. Broad introductory clauses plus subparts are each counted. See examples and case law cited (Jan Bell Marketing, Kellogg, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting multiple issues vs single-issue multi-year/multi-mark requests
rubrics_metrics.description: If an interrogatory requests information concerning more than one issue (e.g., sales and advertising), the Board will count each issue as a separate interrogatory. If it asks for 'all relevant facts' concerning a single issue or the same piece of information across multiple years or marks, it will be counted as a single interrogatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful drafting can reduce counts (frame as single-issue requests); Board will look to substance over form when counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble/instructions not counted but not dispositive for adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Introductory instructions or a preamble to interrogatories will not be counted as interrogatories or subparts for purposes of the 75 limit. However, the Board is not bound by those instructions when determining the adequacy of an answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on preamble language to avoid substantive obligations; the Board will independently assess adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy for belief that interrogatories exceed limit
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party believes the number of interrogatories served exceeds the limit and does not wish to waive that objection, it must, within the time for (and instead of) serving answers and specific objections, serve a general objection on the ground of excessive number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not answer the first 75 and object to the rest. If propounding party files a motion to compel, it must include the set(s) of interrogatories alleged to exceed the limit, show good faith effort to resolve disputes, and comply with § 2.120(e). It is recommended the moving party include its counting method showing the number does not exceed 75.
